quote: ebenso zeige, dass man von der Curve $x^4+y^4=1$ unend lich viele Punkte mit linearen Zirkeln, d.h. durch Wurzelziehn construiren kann und ebenso $\infty$ viele Punkte der Fläche 5ter Ord. $x^5+y^5+z^5=1$. (mit Hilfe der [-Linien[?]-] Haupttangenten).
english: likewise show that one can construct infinitely many points of the curve x^4+y^4=1 with linear circles, i.e. by extracting roots, and likewise infinitely many points of the 5th-order surface x^5+y^5+z^5=1 (with the help of the principal tangents).
topic: A remark that an extensive theory is not a fault even if it is needed to prove a simple theorem, with an analogy to a letter and its reply, followed by notes on finding infinitely many rational points on cubic curves by tangent construction and on extending this to x^4+y^4=1, the quintic surface x^5+y^5+z^5=1, and the diophantine problems of Euler and Legendre.

triage.modern_statement: Read in modern terms, the note asks you to show two things. (a) The Fermat quartic x^4+y^4=1 has infinitely many points whose coordinates are constructible numbers, meaning they lie in iterated quadratic extensions of Q (ruler-and-compass constructions, done by taking square roots). (b) The Fermat quintic surface x^5+y^5+z^5=1 has infinitely many points over such a tower of quadratic fields. For (b), Hilbert suggests a method: at a known point P, take a principal (asymptotic) tangent line. That line meets the surface with multiplicity 3 at P. By Bezout, the remaining 2 intersection points of the degree-5 surface with the line are roots of a quadratic. So they lie in a quadratic extension of the field of definition, and repeating the step produces new points. This continues the earlier note on the page about getting infinitely many rational points on cubics by drawing tangents.
triage.answered_by: No later paper or author resolving this specific note was found. Part (a) is elementary. Pick any rational x with |x|<1; then y=(1-x^4)^{1/4} is obtained by two square roots, which already gives infinitely many constructible real points. Part (b), as Hilbert sets it up with asymptotic tangents, comes down to Bezout plus solving a quadratic. That makes it a geometric exercise or method sketch rather than an open problem. A nearby modern topic does exist: points on Fermat curves over quadratic fields, studied by Aigner, Faddeev and Mordell, and recently over general number fields. But that is the harder question of points over a single quadratic field, not over unlimited towers of quadratic extensions. Two caveats: this is my own reasoning, not taken from a source, and I could only run two searches before hitting the tool limit.

evidence.claim: Quadratic points on the Fermat quartic were studied by Aigner, Faddeev and Mordell. Mordell, knowing there are no non-trivial rational points, studied points over all quadratic fields.
Aigner's result is that only one quadratic field contains non-trivial solutions of the Fermat quartic X^4+Y^4=1. A later paper extends this to X^4+Y^4=2^m.

Recent work shows that over a number field K, the set of K-quadratic points on the Fermat quartic is finite and computable under a stated condition. That differs from points over unlimited iterated quadratic extensions, which is what Hilbert's note is about.
Low-degree algebraic points on Fermat curves remain an active topic. Example: quartic points on the Fermat quintic curve, building on work by Klassen and Tzermias.

triage.why: Allowing arbitrary iterated square roots makes part (a) trivial. Part (b) follows directly from the asymptotic-tangent and Bezout argument Hilbert himself points to, by analogy with the tangent method on cubics. No source treats this note as an open problem, and it is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th. The related research I found concerns points over a fixed quadratic field (Aigner, Faddeev, Mordell, recent arXiv work), which is a different and harder question. This classification rests on my own reading of the mathematics, not on a source discussing this note, and the search was cut short by the tool-use limit. That is why confidence is medium.
